The post Review: Stranahan’s Colorado Whiskey Peated Cask appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Stranahan’s Peated Cask is a distillery exclusive available only at its Denver location. It’s a straightforward single malt which completed its initial aging in virgin American Oak before finishing in various casks that previously held whiskey from Islay as well as local peated casks.

Specifically, the blend includes:

  • 65% whiskey aged 6 to 12 years, finished in Islay casks
  • 35% whiskey aged 8 to 11 years, finished in domestic peated whiskey casks

We got a sizeable sample to check out, so we did.

Stranahan’s Colorado Whiskey Peated Cask Review

To kick things off, the nose here is quite mild. Those expecting a smoke bomb may be disappointed. Those uninterested in smoke-heavy experiences will likely find this wholly approachable. A fairly classic construction of malty cereal, toasted almond, and wet leather finds a rather gentle complement in the form of a beach bonfire smoke and a bit of salty seaweed. The smokiness grows stronger on the nose as it develops in the glass, but it never reaches the point where it becomes remotely overwhelming.

The palate hits with more sweetness than initially expected, that malt becoming almost cookie-like, with vanilla overtones and a vague hint of lemon peel. Enduring and chewy, the whiskey develops in glass to showcase elements of coconut and milk chocolate, infused just so with light layers of smoke, here more indistinct than the clearly maritime elements on the nose. Sweetness develops continuously over the course of the experience; by the end the smoke has nearly disappeared altogether, replaced with more touches of lemon and some light floral notes.

Fun stuff, and worth picking up if you visit one of Stranahan’s locations.

94 proof.

A- / $70

title: Review: Heaven Hill Grain to Glass – Straight Bourbon, Wheated Bourbon, and Rye (Updated 2026)
summary:
Earlier this year, Heaven Hill dropped three unique expressions that take a step away from the distillery’s existing product line — with new mashbills and an approach that focuses foremost on the underlying grains. The launch of the Heaven Hill Grain to Glass series includes three Kentucky whiskeys (at least to start), including a straight…

The post Review: Heaven Hill Grain to Glass – Straight Bourbon, Wheated Bourbon, and Rye (Updated 2026) appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Earlier this year, Heaven Hill dropped three unique expressions that take a step away from the distillery’s existing product line — with new mashbills and an approach that focuses foremost on the underlying grains. The launch of the Heaven Hill Grain to Glass series includes three Kentucky whiskeys (at least to start), including a straight (rye-heavy) bourbon, wheated bourbon, and rye — all over 6 years old. (All three of these samples were distilled in 2017, so they may be up to 7 years old.)

Let’s allow Heaven Hill to give us the deets:

The craft nature of this unique line of Whiskeys starts at the very beginning – the seed. The idea for the line began over 8 years ago as the brainchild of Heaven Hill Executive Chairman Max Shapira. Max’s passion for quality and transparency in whiskey-making lead to a partnership with seed company Beck’s Hybrids – a fellow family-owned and lead operation based in Indiana since 1937. Each year, our Master Distiller works with Beck’s Hybrids to hand select a unique corn seed varietal that has specific attributes desirable for Heaven Hill Grain to Glass, one of which is choosing seed which is best suited for growth in Central Kentucky. The chosen corn seed varietal is then grown by Peterson Farms on one of two sites in Nelson County, one of which is directly across the street from Heaven Hill’s Bardstown facility. Peterson Farms, a multi-generational family farming company, has been entrusted to take the corn seed varietal and cultivate it into healthy grain that goes into the Heaven Hill Grain to Glass mashbills. Since its founding in 1935, Heaven Hill has prided itself on crafting the highest quality Kentucky Whiskeys. Heaven Hill Grain to Glass honors this legacy and the cherished partnerships which were built on handshakes, not contracts.

“Over the course of the nearly 90 years, since the founding of Heaven Hill by my Dad and his brothers, we have always been cognizant of viewing our business from the long term, developing products that fit into this broad vision,” said Heaven Hill Executive Chairman Max Shapira. “Heaven Hill Grain to Glass incorporates everything our long history and heritage brings to our producing what we believe is the most unique, transparent offering that we have brought to market in our entire history. And that is saying a lot.”

The Bourbon and Wheated Bourbon Whiskeys feature mashbills with higher secondary grain content than Heaven Hill’s traditional Bourbon mashbill and Wheated Bourbon mashbill. Bottled at 107 proof, the Kentucky Straight Bourbon Whiskey expression is comprised of 52% corn, 35% rye and 13% malted barley. Bottled at 121 proof, the Kentucky Straight Wheated Bourbon Whiskey expression is made with 52% corn, 35% wheat and 13% malted barley. The Kentucky Straight Rye Whiskey expression is bottled at 123.2, the only barrel proof expression of the series. It also features a higher rye content than Heaven Hill’s traditional Rye Whiskey mashbill consisting of 63% rye, 24% corn and 13% malted barley. The distillates have been aged over six years at Heaven Hill’s Cox’s Creek rickhouse site. Each product is non-chill filtered and bottled at the ideal proof to allow the characteristics of each unique mashbill to shine.

“Working with Beck’s and Peterson Farms to create Grain to Glass has been an incredible experience,” said Master Distiller Conor O’Driscoll. “We’re proud to have crafted an innovative product – taking it from seed to aged liquid – while still remaining true to the values and legacy of Heaven Hill Distillery.”

Well, I’m excited. Let’s see how all that pans out.

We’re updating this review with additional Grain to Glass whiskeys as they arrive. Note that specialty barrel editions of the GtG series are reviewed on their own page.

Heaven Hill Grain to Glass Straight Bourbon 1st Edition (2024) Review

52% corn (Beck’s 6158 varietal), 35% rye, 13% malted barley. Aged 6 years in rickhouse W3 on the 3rd, 4th, and 5th floors. Quite toasty and oaky, with aromatic overtones of roasted grains, mixed fresh herbs (particularly rosemary), and red apple skins. Some nutty walnut shell elements arise with time in glass, along with a substantial tobacco leaf quality. Quite hearty on the palate, with a substantial peanut quality mixing with apple and spice notes — almost like applesauce. The oak remains strong here, as does the rye influence, eventually giving the whiskey an intensely grassy quality and an herbal pop. There’s plenty of lingering peanut butter pushing well into the finish, along with a healthy grind of black pepper and a reprise of clove-heavy baking spice. Very much a frontier-style whiskey that lets the grain do the talking. 107 proof. B / $100 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Heaven Hill Grain to Glass Straight Bourbon 2nd Edition (2025) Review

Similar approach, with the same mash of 52% corn, 35% rye and 13% malt, but the corn seed is varietal Beck’s 6225. Still 6 years old, aged at the Cox’s Creek rickhouse. Note that proof is down 2 ticks to 105. Quite corn-heavy and toasty on the nose, with ample barrel char evident, followed by notes of rosemary and mint. Time in glass really gets the green herbal notes going, and soon enough they overtake everything else. The palate is sweet and earnest — Corn Pops with honey, a touch of charry burnt marshmallow and a fruitiness that takes its time to build — cinnamon spiced apples, then cherry jam, with a solid caramel punch on the back end, ringed with milk chocolate. Ample char informs the finish, adding a bit of grit to what is otherwise a pretty rockin’ whiskey — and one which, aside from a few similarities, doesn’t really resemble the rocky 1st Edition much at all. Namely lacking is that big peanut punch in the 2024 version, and the bold cereal qualities in the first edition are decidedly tempered here. Is it the corn varietal? The rickhouse? The barrel picks? I got nothing, but I would suggest picking this up if you have the 1st Edition on hand (sadly, I don’t) to do a side by side comparison. 105 proof. A- / $100 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Heaven Hill Grain to Glass Wheated Bourbon 1st Edition (2024) Review

52% corn, 35% wheat, 13% malted barley. Quite a different animal, and immediately much more approachable and enticing. The nose features muted spices against an immersive backdrop of honey butter, fresh-cut grass, and cracked black pepper. Increasingly nutty as the whiskey develops in glass, but wholly lacking any overt oakiness. The palate is sweet and, again, loaded with peanut butter and honey notes, with any sense of wood all but hidden away. A light layer of baking spice lingers over a gentle top-note of toasted marshmallow, as a warming heat soothes the throat, evoking notes of hot cocoa. Just a touch of char on the finish. This isn’t a particularly complex bourbon, but it’s a delightful choice for cocktailing — or for deep-diving into what wheated bourbon is all about. I’m not alone here, as this is the only whiskey in the collection that is seeing its price being driven up. 121 proof. A- / $150 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Heaven Hill Grain to Glass Wheated Bourbon 2nd Edition (2025) Review

Same mashbill as last year’s, but made with Beck’s 6225 corn (same as the 2025 straight bourbon). Still aged for over six years at Cox’s Creek, and bottled at barrel proof — considerably lower in abv than the 2024. Soft and nutty on the nose, this doesn’t present itself as even remotely hot, but rather creamy and dessert-like, exuding aromas of crushed almonds, bergamot, pineapple fronds, and a pinch of dark chocolate. Vanilla and caramel create a soothing palate across a creamy body, with a gentle dusting of ground corn to lift the experience. Time spent exploring the whiskey helps notes of toasted coconut, a touch of milky cafe au lait, and ample cinnamon. The finish is actually a bit racy with some red pepper, and more in line with what I’d expect to find in a rye-flavored bourbon, though it is never in disservice of what’s come before. A hint of smoky coffee bean notes linger on the fade-out. Different, but still solid stuff. 106.6 proof. A- / $100 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Heaven Hill Grain to Glass Wheated Bourbon 3nd Edition (2026) Review

This year Heaven Hill dropped three new Grain to Glass releases — all wheated bourbons. We received only the mainline offering; a version aged in French oak barrels and one aged 9 years were also dropped. This year’s whiskey is made with Beck’s 6269 corn but has the same mashbill as 2024 and 2025, spending 6 years in char level #3 barrels at the third, fourth and fifth floors of Warehouses W5 and W6 before bottling. A significant heat kicks things off here, which surprises given this 2026 release is roughly the same abv as last year. Again it’s quite nutty on the nose, but also a little torched, offering aromas of barrel char and clove, followed by coffee grounds. Again this whiskey doesn’t ever connote much of a fruit quality, on nose or palate, remaining with its feet firmly in the realm of torched caramel, chocolate sauce, and pepper. As with the ’25, it hits much closer to a modern rye bourbon than a modern wheater, perhaps owed entirely to the power of those heirloom grains. Water tempers just about everything in the experience, and while that dulls some of its gritty heat, it gives a much more balanced complexion to the whiskey in the end. 107 proof. B+ / $100 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Heaven Hill Grain to Glass Rye 1st Edition (2024) Review

63% rye, 24% corn, 13% malted barley. Take the pungency of the straight bourbon above and double it, and you’re in the realm of this rye. The nose is a pushy powerhouse, intensely herbal and peppery, like walking through a field of just-cut green grass — backed up by a lumberyard that’s been lightly torched around the edges. No surprises on the palate: The impact of the rye is heavy and immediate, and all-encompassing. Many of the bourbon’s same flavor elements appear here but in variations, most of them scorching on the tongue: Rosemary and thyme, burnt pie crust, heavily browned butter, and just a ton of cloves and black pepper to close things out. While the bourbon hints at fruit elements, the rye does not, tamping them down into near-oblivion. It’s as aggressive a rye as you’ll encounter around these parts — and if the idea was to let the grain do all the talking, that has succeeded admirably. 123.2 proof. B / $100 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Heaven Hill Grain to Glass Rye 2nd Edition (2025) Review

A different mashbill than 2024: 63% rye, 20% corn, and 13% malt, made with Beck’s Hybrids 6225 corn grown by Peterson Farms on one of two sites in Nelson County, Kentucky. The distillate went into the barrel at 107 proof and was aged for over six years at Heaven Hill’s Cox’s Creek rickhouse site. Considerably lower in abv than the 2024, also. The construction here is wildly different, and the character of the whiskey is divergent as well. A rye-powered nose offers savory notes, heavy with dill this time out, then almond and honey offering some tempering notes. An undercurrent of smoked meat, menthol, and a lingering hospital character add a bit of distraction. Very herbal on the palate, with loads more dill, the whiskey is bready to a fault — though it’s clearly a bit thinner than the 2024 release, thanks to the lower abv. Fruitier notes in the form of apples, then cherries, are followed by a reprise of menthol. The overall presentation is driven by the heavy herbal element, making this all spice, all the time — with all of its other flavor components mild diversions from its single-minded mission. 105.2 proof. B / $100 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

title: Review: Starlight Bourbon 10 Years Old 2026 and Mizunara Reserve Bourbon
summary:
Starlight Distillery has been firing off luxe releases for a few years now, and we’ve been trying to keep up with this Indiana upstart’s releases. It’s not an easy task, as they roll out at a healthy clip. Jacob offered a deep dive into the operation’s 25th anniversary releases earlier this year. We’re back already…

The post Review: Starlight Bourbon 10 Years Old 2026 and Mizunara Reserve Bourbon appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Starlight Distillery has been firing off luxe releases for a few years now, and we’ve been trying to keep up with this Indiana upstart’s releases. It’s not an easy task, as they roll out at a healthy clip. Jacob offered a deep dive into the operation’s 25th anniversary releases earlier this year. We’re back already with a look at two more new drops that you’re likely to find should you go out seeking Starlight.

Starlight Indiana Straight Bourbon 10 Years Old 2026 Review

Round two of Starlight’s 10 year old bourbon is a ten-barrel blend of Starlight’s two sweet mash mashbills, the same 3-grain and 4-grain bills Jacob outlined last year. Copper pot distilled and entered into barrel at low proof, the barrels were aged in Warehouse #2, West Side, the warmest of Starlight’s rickhouses. Oddly this resulted in a considerably lower final proof than in 2025, though it’s still a barnburner at 57.1% abv.

There’s a ton of fruit on the nose this year, cherry (again) set against a backdrop of black tea and weak coffee. The barrel influence isn’t shy, showcasing plenty of fresh oak and anise, sometimes evoking a grittiness that can be a bit mouth-puckering. Notes of orange peel add some needed fruit, with cracked black pepper adding spice. Time in glass helps cinnamon and cardamom notes to gain prominence, while a splash of water improves the overall balance of the expression.

There’s plenty to admire here, though at $250 and up, the value proposition is decidedly questionable. 114.2 proof. B+ / $250

Starlight Mizunara Reserve Bourbon Review 

It’s not quite the same whiskey as Starlight’s Carl T. Huber’s Mizunara Bourbon — or at least, it’s a different batch, with a different name — and with a slightly lower abv (and the same price). This is crafted from Starlight’s traditional sweet mash (mashbill unstated) and 8 years total of maturation split between new oak before a finishing stretch in Japanese Mizunara oak casks.

A much sweeter spin on the Starlight formula, this engages immediately with notes of chestnut and almond paste, soon evoking a floral quality that evokes wholly fitting thoughts of orange and cherry blossoms. Time in glass takes the glass more into sesame territory with a pinch of cigar box character, altogether making for a much softer aromatic experience than you’re likely to have encountered in the world of bourbondom.

The palate is equally nutty and quite sweet, butterscotch and vanilla caramels all melted together into a flavor that’s light in body, warming, and evocative of holiday time with its late-game flavors of dried fruits, pecans, and warm gingerbread all in a swirl. The gentle fruit notes are indistinct, with a fruit salad character that blends nicely with all that spice. Soothing and warming, it’s definitely my favorite of this duo. 110 proof. Reviewed: Batch #3. A / $150

title: Review: Tequilas of Lagrimas del Valle (Updated 2026)
summary:

It recently launched its fourth and fifth ranch, with 2024’s La Loma and La Sabina joining Palo Verde (2022), El Chiqueño (2022), and El Sabino (2023). La…

The post Review: Tequilas of Lagrimas del Valle (Updated 2026) appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Lágrimas del Valle (“tears of the valley”) launched a few years back with the goal of showcasing “single ranches” of blue agave to showcase how terroir influences tequila. It recently launched its fourth and fifth ranch, with 2024’s La Loma and La Sabina joining Palo Verde (2022), El Chiqueño (2022), and El Sabino (2023). La Loma is the first of the tequilas in the lineup to come from the state of Michoacán. All of Lagrimas’s bottlings are vintage dated with the year of the agave harvest, also.

Here’s a little more detail on production:

Lágrimas del Valle is produced in collaboration with the Rosales Family (of Tequila Cascahuin NOM 1123) and current Master Distiller Salvador “Chava” Rosales Trejo, the third generation of his family. Their distilling tradition dates back to 1904 in El Arenal, Jalisco, Mexico, located within the heart of the “Valley” of Tequila. Each bottling carries a familiar profile but will be distinctly unique in both flavor and aroma.

Lágrimas begins by selecting the very best Single Ranch (Rancho Unico) of blue agave available – looking for ripeness, but also for signs of complexities of flavor. The agaves are then cut, broken down, and loaded into their small 12-16-ton steam powered masonry ovens. Cascahuin utilizes a unique intermittent cooking method for eight hours per day, then stopping until the following day, and repeating over the course of four days. This allows for deep layers of flavor to be developed. The cooked agaves are then removed from the ovens, and their “agua miel” (honey waters) extracted. For Lágrimas, 70% of the agaves are crushed utilizing a roller mill and then fermented in stainless steel tanks, while the other 30% are crushed using a Tahona, and fermented in open air wooden tanks. A unique blend is determined through multiple rounds of blind tastings alongside the family.

“Lágrimas demonstrates that terroir exists in the blue agave and tequila,” said Brandon Cummins, Director of Education, Altamar Brands, which collaborated on the development as well as imports and sells Lágrimas del Valle in the U.S. “While many brands aim to create a consistent profile year over year, Lágrimas embraces the uniqueness of each individual ranch and produces in such a way as to emphasize that distinct character. We do this intentionally, to demonstrate the rich complexity of the Blue Weber Agave.”

Note that Lagrimas only bottles blanco/plata and reposado tequilas, at least for now.

We received a quartet of bottlings, including two from La Loma, one from La Sabina, and one from El Sabino. We’ll delve into all four in the tasting notes that follow.

All expressions are 92 proof. NOM 1123.

Lagrimas del Valle Plata La Loma 2024 Review

Brilliant jalapeno and green pepper on the nose, with overtones of lime. Ground black pepper arrives with some time in glass, followed by a layer of turned earth and saddle leather. The complex palate is quite powerful, showcasing intense herbal notes that are tempered by lemon custard, caramel, and marzipan, making for a very creamy and almost dessert-like quality that’s quite rare to find in a blanco. The pungency of green agave percolates throughout the experience, clinging perhaps too hard on the finish, which comes across as a bit overly gritty and tannic. 92 proof. B+ / $60 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Lagrimas del Valle Reposado La Loma 2024 Review

Aged three months in ex-bourbon barrels. Unbelievably pale, it’s difficult to tell this is reposado once it’s poured in the glass, and the nose doesn’t do much to alter that perception. Again heavy herbal and jalapeno notes are prominent, with overtones of earth, wet leather, and a touch of beefiness that gives the aroma some austerity. It remains plenty peppery on the palate and retains much of the DNA of the Plata, but more vivid layers of marzipan and sesame add an extra layer of creaminess over what’s already visible in the core spirit. A hint of honeydew adds a layer of fruit that emerges with time in glass, with finishing notes of toasted marshmallow and caramel sauce. Turns out three months is plenty of time to temper any roughness out of the blanco spirit. A- / $65 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Lagrimas del Valle Plata El Sabino 2023 Review

Fresher than the La Loma offering, with bright lemon, a smattering of green herbs, a pinch of mint, and some white pepper all imbuing the rich and vibrant nose. The palate stays the course, though a significant peppery quality threatens to push the creamier elements of the tequila out of prominence. Fortunately, they mostly hold the line, showcasing notes of almond milk and touches of vanilla, followed by a hearty burst of juicy mandarin orange, touched with milk chocolate. As with La Loma, there’s a maturity to this unaged tequila that is surprising and unexpected, predominantly visible through its elegant, well-rounded body. A- / $65 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Lagrimas del Valle Reposado La Sabina 2024 Review

Rested 3 months in bourbon barrels. Moderately darker in color than the La Loma reposado. Clear barrel notes kick off on the nose, making this a more iconic example of reposado than La Loma, with its herbal character filtered into the background. Instead, aromas of coconut husk, mint, and sesame oil all offer an initial pungency, before some of that greenery fights its way back into focus. The palate blends sweet and savory, jumping from almond and some toasted cashew notes to green pepper and a hint of scallion. There’s less biting jalapeno here, the tequila coming across as a bit more subdued and well-integrated as gentle waves of pepper waft over the caramel-laced finish. This expression is a bit less complex than some of Lagrimas’s other bottlings, but it never hits a sour note and acquits itself perfectly well as a reposado. A- / $65

Lagrimas del Valle Plata La Mesa del Charco 2025 Review

The first of two expressions from an El Arenal-situated estate. 70% of agaves are crushed with a roller, 30% with a tahona. Fermentation is in open air wooden tanks with the addition of “bagasse,” or agave fibers. Bracing on the nose, this tequila punches hard out of the gate with peppery agave backed by a huge rush of citrus — lime and orange in a twist. That power continues on the palate, though perhaps to a slightly lesser degree, with some gentle earthiness coming into focus. The citrus notes are much better integrated than the nose would suggest, the tequila’s greener elements keeping one foot firmly in the garden. Notes of rosemary and thyme linger, the finish slightly nutty with almond overtones. Outstanding on its own and as versatile as it gets in cocktails. A- / $55

Lagrimas del Valle Reposado La Mesa del Charco 2025 Review

No specific aging information, but the very pale color and the producer’s history indicates it’s probably on the order of 3 months. There’s still plenty of agave character on the nose here, really quite bracing with the peppery attack evident in the blanco expression. Citrus however is a bit muted, replaced by a subtle, wood-driven vanilla quality. The palate is greener than I’d have liked, more in line with the blanco than a traditional reposado, though it’s tempered enough to show off a touch of that vanilla and some milk chocolate notes. Toasted walnut elements develop with time in glass, though things return more toward a herbaceous quality on the finish, the conclusion ultimately falling a bit flat compared to what’s come before. B+ / $60

title: Review: Wines of the Cotes du Rhone, 2026 Releases
summary:

It’s a campaign christened, with blunt minimalism, “Refresh Your Wine.” I somehow find myself uncharacteristically in agreement with their marketing and public relations agencies of record.…

The post Review: Wines of the Cotes du Rhone, 2026 Releases appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
The Côtes du Rhône appellation is taking up a curious evangelism. It is urging the faithful and revival tent-curious to entertain a temptation once considered heretical: chill your reds. It’s a campaign christened, with blunt minimalism, “Refresh Your Wine.” I somehow find myself uncharacteristically in agreement with their marketing and public relations agencies of record. As of this writing, it is late September, and the thermometer has apparently not taken a moment to read the calendar. The heat index persists at triple-digit levels more suited to July’s worst intentions, leaving the fire pit unlit and customary deep reds waiting in the wings for more worthy weather. At this point, I am up for any notion providing some new form of relief or enjoyment. So we beat on, with an open mind and wine fridge, to put three Côtes du Rhône bottlings through their paces. I’m thinking of it as a temporary truce between stalwart conviction and calendar.

2023 La Bastide Saint Dominique Côtes du Rhône – 60% Grenache 40% Syrah. This initially pours out quite unsteady but eventually finds its footing, settling nicely into deep and layered waves of raspberry, currant, wet stone, thyme and crushed violet. Medium-bodied with velvet tannins and good acidity supporting a finish of cola, fresh cherry and a faint note of white pepper. Open this while preparing an easy dinner and, unless you are crafting some ambitious gastronomical monstrosity or heating leftovers in the microwave, it should be ready around the same time. B+ / $15

2022 Château Gigognan Bois des Moines Côtes du Rhône – 60% Grenache and 40% Syrah. Vibrant aromas of red cherry and raspberry open on the nose, with some bay leaf following as it develops, preventing the whole affair from collapsing into jam. A surprisingly silky body carries the red fruit forward, with cranberry, orange zest and a faint touch of chocolate evident on the finish. Chill it or don’t. Either way, it is quite satisfying. A- / $22

2022 Roche-Andran Cuvee Visan Côtes du Rhône – 60% Grenache, 30% Syrah and 10% Mourvèdre. Plenty of Côtes du Rhône’s trademarks on display, with notes of blackberries, graphite and black pepper dominating throughout. Full-bodied with the fruit adding some acidity, but the spices take over on the lingering finish and never relinquish control. Of the trio, this is the singular instance where the gains from a stay in the refrigerator are minimal. B / $20

title: Review: GlenAllachie Palo Cortado Sherry Cask Finish 11 Years Old
summary:
The fourth release in GlenAllachie‘s Sherry Series recently arrived, and it’s an unusual one: This single malt is finished in Palo Cortado casks, which are virtually unheard of in whisky production. Palo Cortado begins as pale Fino sherry that is refortified to about 35 proof, which kills the flor yeast and promotes the oxidation of…

The post Review: GlenAllachie Palo Cortado Sherry Cask Finish 11 Years Old appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
The fourth release in GlenAllachie‘s Sherry Series recently arrived, and it’s an unusual one: This single malt is finished in Palo Cortado casks, which are virtually unheard of in whisky production. Palo Cortado begins as pale Fino sherry that is refortified to about 35 proof, which kills the flor yeast and promotes the oxidation of the wine. GlenAllachie describes the resulting flavor as sitting “between Amontillado and Oloroso, combining the aromatic finesse of the former with the structure, body and richness of the latter.”

The whisky carries an 11 year old age statement but there’s no detail on the length of the sherry finishing. Initial maturation takes place in standard ex-bourbon barrels.

Let’s give it a try.

GlenAllachie Palo Cortado Sherry Cask Finish 11 Years Old Review

The intense nuttiness of the Palo Cortado is on immediate display here, and in the glass it comes across as far more intense than any Amontillado (or Amontillado-finished whiskey) I’ve sampled in my career. Gently mushroomy, with a hint of oxidized red wine visible, the nose adds an intensely savory quality to the proceedings, notes of green beans and spring onion lying faint in the distance, serving to amplify the brooding earthiness that dominates.

The palate melds that nutty, pastoral, savory quality with some of the cereal sweetness you expect from a younger single malt. Chewy and grainy, these are two sides of a coin, driven first by toasted almond and walnut elements, then a note of gently honeyed sesame cake. The sweetness is never extreme, but it’s enough to keep the whisky alive — and from falling victim to what could otherwise take things too far into fields. Flashes of citrus evoke thoughts of Oloroso, if fleetingly.

The finish is short to moderate in length and quite sharp, reprising its nutty attack before perking up with some mocha elements and, at last, a healthy pinch of baking spice. This alone is enough to elevate the whisky into a new territory that emerges as the best part of the experience — gently spicy but with enough gravitas to keep things from spiraling into overt sweetness. I polished off my (significant) sample before I knew it. Solidly priced, too.

96 proof.

A- / $84

summary:

The post Review: Smolbol Peanut + Cassava Snacks appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Peanuts are one of the most iconic bar snack items of all time. They’re also one of the most boring bar snack items of all time. Brazil figured out how to spice them up, wrapping the shelled nut in cassava starch, compressing it into a crunchy shell.

Say hello to Smolbol, the cleverly named snack that you can add to your happy hour regimen if you’re looking for something a little different.

Smolbols vary in size from about the size of a “Goobers” chocolate-covered peanut to a gumball, and they’re available in five (largely self-explanatory) flavors: sea salt, garlic parmesan, barbecue, chili lime, and cheddar cheese. Each comes in 6 oz. packs for about 8 bucks a pop. The sea salt flavor was not nearly salty enough, but enjoyed all the others, with either cheddar or BBQ my favorite, depending on the day.

The Smolbol experience is a curious one: After a quite satisfying crunchy pop — which releases the peanut inside — the Smolbol’s cassava shell quickly dissolves. That shell then solidifies in your molars, almost like a paste, and getting it out can be either a fun afterparty to the main event or a real pain, depending on your perspective.

In the end, after eating nearly two pounds of Smolbols, I found that they really did grow on me. The flavors are surprisingly mild: Every one of them could have used at least twice as much seasoning, and the sea salt expression really didn’t taste like anything at all, unfortunately. Despite that, I found myself gravitating to the spherical oddities at snack time more often than not — invariably with a hearty, liquid chaser to help with the teeth cleaning.

each $8 per 6 oz. bag [BUY IT NOW FROM AMAZON]

title: Review: Dark Arts Sherry Garcia Bourbon Vol. 3
summary:
There is a certain kind of bourbon drinker who does not simply buy whiskey. They follow it. They track releases, compare batches, trade bottles, swap information and know exactly which distillery produced what, where a particular barrel came from and when the next release is expected. Give them a scarce bottle from a whiskey maker…

The post Review: Dark Arts Sherry Garcia Bourbon Vol. 3 appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
There is a certain kind of bourbon drinker who does not simply buy whiskey. They follow it. They track releases, compare batches, trade bottles, swap information and know exactly which distillery produced what, where a particular barrel came from and when the next release is expected. Give them a scarce bottle from a whiskey maker they trust, and they will go looking for it.

That kind of devotion should sound familiar to anyone who has spent time around Grateful Dead fans.

Deadheads built a culture around following the band, collecting recordings, trading information and showing up again and again, sometimes traveling considerable distances to be part of the experience. The music was certainly at the center of it, but the community surrounding the band became its own phenomenon. For many fans, being a Deadhead was about far more than owning a few albums. It was about participation.

There is a similar spirit among the followers of Dark Arts Whiskey House. The bourbon world has no shortage of whiskey, but Dark Arts has managed to build its own devoted following, one release at a time. Its bottles have become objects of pursuit for drinkers who pay attention to what the whiskey house is doing and are eager to see what comes next.

Which brings us to a bottle with a name that could hardly be more appropriate for this particular comparison.

In the fall of 2026, Dark Arts Whiskey House released Volume 3 of Sherry Garcia Bourbon. Jerry Garcia’s name does not appear on the bottle, but “Sherry Garcia” is close enough to make the joke immediately apparent. The name works because the bourbon has been finished in Oloroso sherry casks, giving Dark Arts a reason to turn a whiskey release into a playful nod to the Grateful Dead’s legendary guitarist.

And perhaps that is where the comparison between Deadheads and bourbon obsessives gets particularly interesting. Both groups have spent years proving that following something can be as important as simply possessing it. There is always another show, another recording, another bottle, another release. You can chase it, study it, talk about it and argue about it with people who are just as invested as you are.

Volume 3 starts with bourbon distilled by MGP in Lawrenceburg, Indiana, from a mashbill of 60% corn, 36% rye and 4% malted barley. The label states that the bourbon is at least 8.5 years old, though the blend ranges from bourbon aged for 8 years and 9 months to bourbon aged for 9 years and 10 months.

That bourbon then underwent secondary maturation in 22 Oloroso sherry casks, each holding 59 gallons. The Oloroso casks were filled over a period stretching from November 2024 through March 2026.

Dark Arts’ latest release sits at the intersection of two particularly devoted tribes. One follows whiskey. The other follows Jerry Garcia and the Grateful Dead. Both know a thing or two about chasing the next thing down the road.

Is Volume 3 of Sherry Garcia something for which the bourbon community can be grateful?

Or is it dead on arrival?

Let’s find out.

Dark Arts Sherry Garcia Bourbon Vol. 3 (2026) Review

The nose opens with dried cranberries, and very dry ones at that, with little of their original moisture remaining. The cranberry note is prominent, more akin to the dusty aroma of fully dried fruit, followed by dense chocolate fudge that brings plenty of creaminess. As the bourbon opens in the glass, charred orange peel and very dark caramel begin to show.

The overall nose is exceptionally well integrated. The Oloroso sherry never becomes overwhelming, while the chocolate avoids veering into excessive tannin.

The palate brings plenty of red fruit, but in a much brighter form: maraschino cherry syrup. It is an unusually bright, sweet cherry note given the dark dried cherry profile found on the nose. Orange peel joins the cherry, followed by roasted hazelnuts and milk chocolate through the mid-palate. Taken together, those flavors present something remarkably close to the composite profile of Nutella, all wrapped in a very dense mouthfeel.

The finish brings the bourbon back toward the profile established on the nose, with dried cherry joining dark chocolate. The chocolate is less sweet here than the fudge presented on the nose, while clove adds a healthy dose of spice. Toasted pecans bring another layer of oak influence to the finish.

This is easily one of the more enjoyable Oloroso sherry finishes I have experienced, with impressive consistency from the first aroma through the final sip. For anyone looking for a top-notch example of an Oloroso sherry-finished bourbon, this is it.

114.06 proof.

A / $100

title: Review: Wines of San Felice, 2026 Releases
summary:
San Felice is one of our favorite Italian wine producers, the brand creating a wide range of wines from throughout Tuscany — though primarily Chianti Classico. Today we look at five 2026 releases from the producer, all excellent and well worth your while. 2024 San Felice In Avane Chardonnay Toscana IGT – A new wine…

The post Review: Wines of San Felice, 2026 Releases appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
San Felice is one of our favorite Italian wine producers, the brand creating a wide range of wines from throughout Tuscany — though primarily Chianti Classico.

Today we look at five 2026 releases from the producer, all excellent and well worth your while.

2024 San Felice In Avane Chardonnay Toscana IGT – A new wine to me, this is a rather brooding expression of chardonnay. The restrained offering finds itself a bit bitter on the attack, notes of lime leaf tucking in to underripe apple, white florals, and lemon curd as the palate develops. The expected breakthrough into more exuberant fruitiness along with some salinity on the finish never really arrives, the affair stopping short before it feels like things really get going. Flashes of interest, however. B+ / $40

2023 San Felice Borgo Chianti Classico DOCG – Iconic Chianti, this offers a bright, cherry-fueled attack that is laced through and through with green herbs, hints of anise, and some dark chocolate. Ample acidity keeps the wine lively and refreshing, with citrusy notes developing as the finish approaches. There’s lemon and orange peel here, evoking thoughts of mostarda and cut grass. Quite versatile and lovely throughout. A- / $40

2022 San Felice Pugnitello Toscana IGT – Punchy and driven by tobacco and dark chocolate notes, San Felice (which is one of the premiere developers of pugnitello) has refined this grape to showcase its more savory characteristics — heavy on licorice, tobacco, light touches of tar — while simultaneously allowing fruit to peek through the cracks. Black cherry, blackberry, and late-game rhubarb all offer a juicy but almost wintry quality to the wine, though intense acidity and more moderated tannins keep everything both tight and lively. I’d hold this for a few years just to see what happens. A- / $95

2022 San Felice Il Grigio Chianti Classico Riserva DOCG – Surprisingly more fruit-forward than expected for a Riserva level Chianti Classico, this unabashedly cherry-fueled offers gentle tertiary notes of cloves and a touch of black tea, before a brighter raspberry-fueled finish comes into focus. Any licorice notes on the finish are more candied, fitting in perfectly with the theme to date. A- / $37

2021 San Felice Campogiovanni Brunello di Montalcino DOCG – A thick and slightly raisiny wine with chocolate overtones, this Brunello leans richer than is typical, its cherry and wild berry notes comparatively muted. Dark caramel and even more chocolate notes build from there, leading to a gravelly charcoal and toasty anise conclusion. The overtly oxidized sweetness, almost date-lake, becomes thick on the finish, finding a foil in a heavy layer of vanilla. The palate ends up all but coated with the extracted, almost jammy character. A bit too heavy for me. B+ / $84

2022 San Felice La Pieve Chianti Classico Gran Selezione DOCG – As with Borgo, this presents a classic Chianti structure — tightly wound cherry, layered tannins, and modest spice to even it all out. The anise is lightened up, which lets the chocolate character fire more freely, notes of graphite and turned earth both becoming prominent as the finish emerges. For all its depth of flavor, the wine is surprisingly straightforward, never deviating from its mission, though the cherry turns more toward blackberry on the lengthy, exuberant, and wholly enjoyable finish. Sometimes, a seamless through-line works out just fine. A / $95

They also increased their distribution footprint to include whiskey-hungry Florida and Illinois. And they remain, as ever, dedicated to…

The post Review: New Riff Malted Rye Sherry Finish Barrel Proof (Updated 2026) appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
New Riff Distillery hasn’t been slowing down one bit. They recently completed a significant expansion at their Newport, Kentucky distillery, increasing production capacity by 50%, and they’ve added the necessary barrel warehousing at a nearby site. They also increased their distribution footprint to include whiskey-hungry Florida and Illinois. And they remain, as ever, dedicated to making what they call “whiskey riffs.” The latest, however, is actually a riff on a riff. I’ll let them explain:

“Last year we released our Malted Rye Whiskey, and experiencing its remarkably elegant, sophisticated character gave us another idea,” said co-founder Jay Erisman. “We think of it as a malt whiskey first and a rye whiskey second, which raised the question: what would happen if we treated it like other malt whiskies and aged it in sherry casks?”

New Riff’s first batches of 100% Malted Rye Whiskey were distilled in 2014, and the initial release landed in May 2021. For this sherry finished elaboration, New Riff imported custom-made 53-gallon Spanish sherry casks and filled them with 5-year-old New Riff Malted Rye Whiskey. Twelve oloroso and three Pedro Ximenez casks were filled with whiskey and aged another year, before being vatted in the fall of 2021 and left to marry and condition together for several following months until they were bottled in spring of 2022 (at cask strength).

The distillery has put out no shortage of winning “riffs” in recent years, including the malted rye at the heart of this expression. Let’s see how the latest edition stacks up.

Update: We’re adding fresh coverage of this re-released whiskey to expand this review.

New Riff Malted Rye Sherry Finish Barrel Proof (2022) Review

The sherry finishing and higher proof have definitely added some heft to the aroma compared to the standard malted rye with ample spice cabinet and leathery notes of dark berries and sweet almond paste. The sherry isn’t overpowering though, and things remain fairly wood-driven with cinnamon stick and toasty barrel char growing more prominent as it opens in the glass. The palate showcases even more sweet sherry character with bold, syrupy notes of blackberry cobbler and raspberry candies. The rye spice is unusually a bit more prominent than in the original, with black pepper and clove popping on the mid-palate and segueing to a generous finish of cooked red fruits, some mild oaky astringency, and lingering notes of tobacco and cherry juice.

Like past limited editions, this bottle was made available only to New Riff’s Whiskey Club and select retailers. However, the success of Malted Rye last year has landed it in the New Riff core lineup, so perhaps we will be seeing even more of this sherry-finished expression in the future. 112.7 proof. A- / $65 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

New Riff Malted Rye Sherry Finish Barrel Proof (2026) Review

A few small changes: The previous release started with 5-year-old malted rye and this year’s whiskey started as 6-year-old malted rye. Both were finished in oloroso and Pedro Ximénez sherry casks. Both hit the bottle at cask strength but this year’s release is 2.5% stronger.

The nose of this reissued offering is big and sings both rye and sherry notes at full volume. Raisin and cinnamon sticks hit first, wrapped in leather. Raspberry compote comes next along with caramel and some clove. A touch of cereal grain follows through at the end.

Sipped neat, the whiskey hits hard. In his review four years ago, Drew noted that the rye spices are bolder in this finished whiskey than they are in the unfinished rye, and that is absolutely still the case in the newest release. Sharp cinnamon, fresh cracked black pepper, and clove come bursting out of the glass along with an alcohol bite. Immediately following come sherry notes including raspberry preserves, blackberry, and caramel. Midpalate brings some vanilla to the mix, which stays through the long finish. The good folks at New Riff recommend adding water to bring out the sherry notes or abstaining to highlight the rye. I gave both a try, and it’s true, but the rye notes never disappeared with the addition of water.

Altogether, this a well crafted whiskey that deserves serious attention from fans of both rye whiskey and sherry-finished single malts. -RL 117.3 proof. A- / $70
